cards.front: Recall a key point about Angels
cards.back: Muslims believe angels (mala'ikah) are created from light and serve as God's messengers. They have no free will — they always obey Allah. Belief in angels is one of the Six Articles of Faith in Sunni Islam.

cards.front: What should you know about rs exam tips — angels?
cards.back: 1. For Angels questions, always include specific scriptural or source references where relevant 2. Explain both religious and non-religious viewpoints 3. Use specialist vocabulary precisely (e.g. terms from the specification) 4. Evaluate by analysing strengths and weaknesses of different views before reaching your conclusion 5. Link your discussion of Angels to its real-world impact on believers and society

cards.front: What should you know about uk context?
cards.back: In the UK, the concept of guardian angels provides comfort to many British Muslims. The belief that two angels record all deeds motivates ethical behaviour: a Muslim knows that even secret actions are witnessed and will be accounted for on the Day of Judgement.

cards.front: What should you know about uk context?
cards.back: The distinction between angels (who obey perfectly) and humans (who can choose to obey or disobey) is central to the Islamic understanding of morality. Humans are morally superior to angels when they choose good, because their choice involves overcoming temptation — an option angels do not face.

cards.front: What should you know about uk context?
cards.back: During the COVID-19 pandemic, many British Muslims found comfort in the belief that Allah’s angels were watching over them. Imams reminded congregations that the recording angels witnessed both their patience in hardship and their kindness to others during the crisis.
Chief angel; brought revelation (e.g. Brought the Qur'an to Muhammad over 23 years; announced the birth of Isa (Jesus) to Maryam)
Controls weather and natural forces (e.g. Sends rain, wind and provision for the earth; responsible for the forces of nature)
Will blow the trumpet on the Day of Judgement (e.g. Signals the end of the world and the resurrection of the dead)
Angel of death (e.g. Removes the soul from the body at the time of death)

cards.front: What does Munkar and Nakir mean?
cards.back: Question the dead in the grave (e.g. Ask the deceased about their faith; test their belief in Allah and Muhammad)

cards.front: What does Raqib and Atid mean?
cards.back: Record human deeds (e.g. Raqib records good deeds; Atid records bad deeds — the books of record used on the Day of Judgement)

Students often confuse Sunni and Shi'a beliefs about predestination. Wrong: "All Muslims believe everything is predestined and humans have no free will." Correct: "Most Muslims believe God has foreknowledge but humans have free will to choose; the balance between predestination and free will is understood differently across traditions."
